Succoth
SUK-oth
proper noun
Hebrew Sukkoth, “booths” or “shelters,” from sukkah, a booth; a town in the Jordan valley east of the river.

See also: Succoth · Succoth

Biblical Definition

Succoth was a town in the valley of the Jordan, east of the river, in the portion of Gad (Josh 13:27). It took its name from the booths that Jacob made there: returning from Padan-aram after his wrestling at Peniel, Jacob journeyed to Succoth, and built him a house, and made booths for his cattle, “therefore the name of the place is called Succoth” (Gen 33:17). In the days of the judges, when Gideon pursued the kings of Midian with his three hundred faint yet pursuing, the men of Succoth refused to give bread to his weary band, mocking his unfinished victory; and when Gideon returned in triumph he chastised them, teaching the elders of the city with thorns of the wilderness and with briers (Judg 8:5–16). In Solomon’s reign the vessels of brass for the temple were cast in the clay ground of the Jordan plain between Succoth and Zarthan (1Ki 7:46). The name “booths” recalls the feast of tabernacles, when Israel dwelt in booths to remember the wilderness pilgrimage. Succoth witnesses both to the pilgrim life of God’s people, who have here no continuing city, and to the danger of withholding kindness from the LORD’s servants in the day of their labour.

Webster 1828 Definition

A town in the Jordan valley named for Jacob’s booths; where the men refused bread to Gideon’s weary band.

expand to see more

SUCCOTH, a town in the valley of the Jordan, east of the river, in Gad.

Jacob built booths for his cattle there, and so named the place (Gen 33:17).

The men of Succoth refused bread to Gideon’s weary band (Judg 8:5).

Gideon chastised its elders with thorns and briers (Judg 8:16).

The temple vessels were cast in the clay ground near it (1Ki 7:46).

Key Scripture

Gen 33:17 — "And Jacob journeyed to Succoth, and built him an house, and made booths for his cattle: therefore the name of the place is called Succoth."

Judg 8:7 — "And Gideon said, Therefore when the LORD hath delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into mine hand, then I will tear your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers."

Judg 8:16 — "And he took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth."

1Ki 7:46 — "In the plain of Jordan did the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarthan."

Modern Corruption

A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson joins the pilgrim life to the duty of kindness to God’s servants.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the warning of the men of Succoth, who withheld bread from Gideon’s faint band because they doubted his victory and feared the Midianites more than they honoured the LORD’s deliverer. To refuse kindness to the servants of God in the day of their labour, out of unbelief or self-interest, is no light thing; Gideon returned and taught them with briers. He that giveth a cup of cold water to a disciple shall not lose his reward, and he that refuses it answers for the slight.

Succoth, “booths,” also recalls the pilgrim character of God’s people. Jacob made booths there, temporary shelters for a journeying man; and Israel kept the feast of booths to remember that they were strangers and sojourners. The believer too dwells in booths, having here no continuing city, but seeking one to come. The name itself preaches that this world is a place of pilgrimage, not of permanent rest.

Hebrew Roots

The name means “booths” or “shelters,” from sukkah, the booth of the feast of tabernacles.

expand to see more

Succoth — Hebrew Sukkoth, “booths” or “shelters.”

The singular sukkah is the booth of the feast of tabernacles.

Jacob named the place for the booths he made for his cattle.

It lay in the Jordan valley in the portion of Gad.

The town of booths preaches the pilgrim life of God’s people.

Usage

"Like the men of Succoth, those who withhold kindness from God’s servants answer for the slight."

"Succoth, the town of booths, teaches that the believer dwells as a pilgrim with no continuing city."

"Gideon’s briers at Succoth warn against doubting the LORD’s deliverer in the day of his labour."
